newsitem.title: DUBAI: Nurses' families visit them in Saudi jail.
newsitem.headline: Nurses' families visit them in Saudi jail.

text.p: Families of two British nurses charged with murder in Saudi Arabia have visited them in prison for an emotional reunion days before their first court appearance in three weeks, their lawyer said on Friday.

The parents of Lucille McLauchlan and sister and brother-in-law of Deborah Parry saw the nurses in prison in Dammam near the eastern oil city of Dhahran on Thursday, said Saudi lawyer Salah al-Hejailan.
It was the families' fourth prison visit since McLauchlan, 31, and Parry, 38, were arrested shortly after the murder of Australian colleague Yvonne Gilford, 55, in Dhahran in December.
Gilford was found stabbed 13 times, bludgeoned and suffocated in her room at the King Fahd military medical complex just days before her birthday.
McLauchlan and Parry, who have withdrawn what they said were forced confessions and professed their innocence, are due to appear in court in nearby Khobar on Sunday.
Hejailan said earlier this week the hearing could lead to the confessions being thrown out.
"It was in good spirit," Hejailan said of Thursday's prison visit. "But they (the families) expressed their extreme anguish and extreme disappointment with the position of Mr Gilford."
Frank Gilford, the victim's brother, has called for the death penalty, traditionally enforced in Saudi Arabia by public beheading by the sword.
Islamic sharia law allows the victim's family to demand the death penalty if the court finds the women guilty and says capital punishment is appropriate.
Three people were beheaded on Friday -- this time for drug smuggling -- but convicted murderers have also been among the 72 people, one of them a woman, executed so far this year.

"While they maintain his intervention will not be needed because their daughters are not guilty, they are innocent, they feel that he and his lawyers are responsible for the delay over technicalities and going back and forth in procedural matters which has caused them extreme hardship in prison and has affected their morale for no good reason," Hejailan said.

Speaking by telephone from his hotel in London, the lawyer told Reuters: "They say very bluntly that if Mr Gilford is so much a believer in the death penalty he should try to change it and introduce it in his own country before he makes use of it in another country."
Hejailan said the families hoped to be allowed to attend the next court hearing on Sunday and would remain in the kingdom until Wednesday. Journalists are barred from the court.
He said the nurses hoped that the judge would nullify the confessions in which they referred to a lesbian relationship. "They are denying it very strongly," he said.
The lawyer said that if the court, which adjourned on July 7 for deliberation, nullified the confessions the case could be shelved or dismissed.
"It is more likely for the judge to open the case for other evidence, if there is any."
Hejailan said Peter Watson, a Scottish lawyer who was an expert on forensic evidence, also attended the prison reunion.
